# GUI Programming {#appendix-a-gui-programming}

Introduction to GUI Programming {#introduction-to-gui-programming}
-------------------------------

The purpose of this appendix is not to teach you how to do Graphical
User Interfaces. It is simply meant to show how writing graphical
applications is the same as writing other applications, just using an
additional library to handle the graphical parts. As a programmer you
need to get used to learning new libraries. Most of your time will be
spent passing data from one library to another.

The GTK Library {#the-gtk-library}
---------------

GTK is the library that draws the windows, buttons and menus of the
GNOME desktop and of many other Linux programs. It is written in C, on
top of GLib, a library of general-purpose functions and data structures
that GTK and GNOME share. GNOME is one of several projects to provide a
complete desktop to Linux users, with a panel to launch applications,
standard applications for file management, settings and many other
things, and libraries for creating applications which fit in with the
way the rest of the system works. This appendix uses version 4 of GTK.

One thing to notice about the GTK library is that it constantly creates
and gives you pointers to large data structures, but you never need to
know how they are laid out in memory. All manipulation of the GUI data
structures is done entirely through function calls. This is a
characteristic of good library design. Libraries change from version to
version, and so does the data that each data structure holds. If you had
to access and manipulate that data yourself, then when the library is
updated you would have to modify your programs to work with the new
library, or at least recompile them. When you access the data through
functions, the functions take care of knowing where in the structure
each piece of data is. The pointers you receive from the library are
*opaque* - you don\'t need to know specifically what the structure they
are pointing to looks like, you only need to know the functions that
will properly manipulate it. When designing libraries, even for use
within only one program, this is a good practice to keep in mind.

This appendix will not go into details about how GTK works. If you would
like to know more, visit the [GTK documentation][AA-GTK-docs] and the
[GNOME developer documentation][AA-1]. They contain tutorials, API
documentation, and everything else you need to start programming in the
GNOME environment. The functions are described with C prototypes, which
you can read as we did in
[Chapter 8](08-sharing-functions-with-code-libraries.qmd#finding-information-about-libraries).

A Simple GTK Program in Two Languages {#a-simple-gtk-program-in-two-languages}
-------------------------------------

This program will simply show a window that has a button to quit the
application. When that button is clicked it will ask you if you are
sure, and if you click Yes it will close the application. To run this
program, type in the following as `0AA-01-gtk-example.s`:

```{.gnuassembler .numberLines include=resource/asm/0AA-01-gtk-example.s}
```

To build this application, you need the development files of GTK 4 (on
Ubuntu, the package `libgtk-4-dev`). Execute the following commands:

```{.bash}
as --64 -g -o 0AA-01-gtk-example.o 0AA-01-gtk-example.s
gcc -o 0AA-01-gtk-example 0AA-01-gtk-example.o $(pkg-config --libs gtk4)
```

Then type in `./0AA-01-gtk-example` to run it.

This time we link with `gcc` instead of `ld`, and the program starts at
`main` instead of `_start`. GTK uses many libraries (`pkg-config
--libs gtk4` prints the `-l` options for all of them), and it expects
the start-up code of the C library, which prepares the program before
calling `main(argc, argv)`. `gcc` adds that code and the dynamic linker
for us; it doesn\'t compile anything here, it only runs `ld` with the
right options. `main` is a normal function: it receives `argc` in _%rdi_
and `argv` in _%rsi_, and returns the exit status in _%rax_. And since
`gcc` makes a PIE program, everything in it must be position-independent
(see
[Chapter 8](08-sharing-functions-with-code-libraries.qmd#position-independent-code)):
all the data is reached relative to _%rip_, and the table `answers`,
which holds addresses, goes in the section `.data.rel.ro`, where the
dynamic linker can write those addresses when the program starts.

This program, like most GUI programs, makes heavy use of passing
pointers to functions as parameters. In this program you create widgets
with the GTK functions and then you set up functions to be called when
certain events happen. These functions are called *callback*
functions. All of the event processing is handled by the function
`g_application_run`, so you don\'t have to worry about how the events
are being processed. All you have to do is have callbacks set up to wait
for them. Our callbacks are normal functions too, called by GTK with the
System V convention, so they must follow all of its rules: parameters in
_%rdi_, _%rsi_ and _%rdx_, callee-saved registers preserved, and
_%rsp_ aligned to 16 at every `call`. That is why each callback pushes
_%rbx_ and _%r12_ (two registers keep the alignment) before it uses
them, and why `main` subtracts 8 more bytes after its three pushes.

Here is a short description of all of the GTK functions that were used
in this program:

gtk_application_new:

:   Creates a new application, and returns a pointer to it. Takes the
    application id (a name in the reverse-domain style, unique for each
    application) and some flags (0 for the default behavior).

g_signal_connect_data:

:   This is the function that connects objects and their signal
    handling callback functions. In C, programs use `g_signal_connect`,
    but it is a macro, a name that the C compiler replaces with a call
    to `g_signal_connect_data` with two more parameters (both 0 here),
    so in assembly language we have to call the real function. It takes
    the object pointer, the name of the signal, the callback function,
    an extra data pointer, a function to free that data (NULL) and some
    flags (0). After this function is called, any time the given event
    is triggered, the callback will be called with the object that
    produced the signal and the extra data pointer.

g_application_run:

:   This function causes GTK to enter into its main loop, the *event
    loop*. GTK checks for events and calls the appropriate callback
    functions when they occur. It starts by emitting the signal
    `activate`, which calls our `activate_handler`, and it continues to
    process events until the application has no windows left or
    `g_application_quit` is called. It returns the exit status.

g_object_unref:

:   GTK objects count how many pointers to them are in use (*reference
    counting*, see the exercises of
    [Chapter 9](09-intermediate-memory-topics.qmd#going-further-7)).
    This function says that we no longer use our pointer; the object is
    freed when nobody uses it.

gtk_application_window_new:

:   Creates a new window that belongs to the application.

gtk_window_set_title:

:   Sets the text in the title bar of a window.

gtk_window_set_default_size:

:   Sets the width and the height of a window, in pixels.

gtk_button_new_with_label:

:   Creates a new button and returns a pointer to it. Takes one
    argument - the text that is in the button.

gtk_window_set_child:

:   This takes a pointer to a window and whatever widget you want (a
    button in this case) and makes the widget be the contents of the
    window.

gtk_window_present:

:   Shows a window, with everything in it.

gtk_alert_dialog_new:

:   Creates a dialog that shows a message. Like `printf`, its first
    parameter is a format, followed by a variable number of parameters,
    so _%al_ must be 0 when we call it.

gtk_alert_dialog_set_buttons:

:   Sets the buttons of the dialog: it takes a list of addresses of
    strings, ended by NULL.

gtk_alert_dialog_set_default_button, gtk_alert_dialog_set_cancel_button:

:   Choose the button that the Return key and the Escape key press: Yes
    (button 0) and No (button 1).

gtk_alert_dialog_choose:

:   Shows the dialog over a window, as a *modal* dialog: in GUI
    programming, a modal window is one that prevents the use of other
    windows (here, the main window) until it is closed. It doesn\'t wait
    for the answer. It returns at once, and when the user clicks on a
    button, GTK calls the function we gave it (`response_handler`) with
    the dialog, a pointer to the result and our extra data. This is an
    *asynchronous* function: the event loop keeps running, and the
    window keeps redrawing itself, while the dialog is open.

gtk_alert_dialog_choose_finish:

:   Called in `response_handler`, it returns the number of the button
    that was clicked.

gtk_window_get_application, g_application_quit:

:   Find the application of a window, and make it leave its event loop
    at the earliest opportunity, so that `g_application_run` returns.

Finally, we have a version in Python, with PyGObject, the Python
interface to GLib and GTK (on Ubuntu, the packages `python3-gi` and
`gir1.2-gtk-4.0`). Type it in as `0AA-01-gtk-example.py`:

```{.python .numberLines include=resource/asm/0AA-01-gtk-example.py}
```

To run it type `python3 0AA-01-gtk-example.py`.

Compare the two versions. They call the same functions, in the same
order, with the same parameters: PyGObject reads the description of
every GTK function from the *introspection* data that GTK installs (the
package `gir1.2-gtk-4.0`), and calls it with the calling convention, as
`ctypes` did in
[Chapter 8](08-sharing-functions-with-code-libraries.qmd#calling-assembly-from-rust-and-python).
Python takes care of the registers, the alignment, the list of buttons
ended by NULL, the `_data` version of `g_signal_connect` and the calls
to `g_object_unref`. In the assembly language version, all of that is
our job.

To test this appendix without a screen, the book\'s `test.bash` runs
both versions in a virtual X server (`Xvfb`), and `xdotool` clicks on
the button and presses Escape (No: the program keeps running), then
clicks again and presses Return (Yes: the program ends with status 0).

GUI Builders {#gui-builders}
------------

In the previous example, you have created the user-interface for the
application by calling the create functions for each widget and placing
it where you wanted it. However, this can be quite burdensome for more
complex applications. Many programming environments, including GTK,
let you describe the user interface in a file instead. GTK reads
descriptions written in XML (`.ui` files) with its `GtkBuilder`, and
there are GUI builders, such as Cambalache, that let you draw the
windows with the mouse and save them in that format. You just have to
write the code for the signal handlers and for initializing your
program.

There are GUI builders for most programming environments. The Qt
library, used by the KDE desktop, has Qt Designer, and the toolkits of
Windows and macOS come with their own.

There is a broad range of choices for developing graphical applications,
but hopefully this appendix gave you a taste of what GUI programming is
like.
